title: What Sunday Really Looked Like in 1950s America

scenes.text: There was a time when Sunday in America felt completely different from every other day of the week. The stores were closed. The streets were quiet. Church bells rang across town. Families dressed in their best clothes, sat down to a big dinner, and spent the afternoon together, doing almost nothing at all. If you grew up in the fifties, you remember that feeling. Sunday was a day apart.
scenes.caption: A DAY APART

scenes.text: Today, Sunday is just another day for many of us. We shop, run errands, answer emails and watch the game. But in the nineteen fifties, Sunday had its own rhythm, its own rules and its own sounds. And for millions of Americans, it was the best day of the week.
scenes.caption: ITS OWN RHYTHM

scenes.text: So let's spend a Sunday in nineteen fifty-six, hour by hour, from the first church bell in the morning to the last television show at night. If you were there, I think you'll smell the pot roast before we're done.
scenes.caption: HOUR BY HOUR

scenes.text: Sunday morning started a little later than a weekday, but not much. Mothers were up early, putting the roast in the oven before church. Fathers read the thick Sunday newspaper, with its sections and sections, and the colored comics that children grabbed first. Dick Tracy, Blondie, Li'l Abner, Prince Valiant and Peanuts.
scenes.caption: THE SUNDAY FUNNIES

scenes.text: Breakfast on Sunday was often special too. Pancakes, waffles, or eggs with bacon and sausage. In some homes, Dad made breakfast on Sundays, the only day of the week he cooked. In others, families who were going to take communion skipped breakfast entirely, and the children's stomachs growled all through the sermon.
scenes.caption: SUNDAY BREAKFAST

scenes.text: Then came the scramble to get everyone dressed. Sunday clothes were special, kept just for church. Boys wore white shirts, clip-on ties and stiff shoes that pinched. Girls wore starched dresses, white socks, patent leather shoes and maybe white gloves and a little hat. Their mothers wore hats too, and gloves, and their best dress.
scenes.caption: SUNDAY CLOTHES

scenes.text: Fathers wore suits and polished shoes, often shined on Saturday night. Hair was combed and slicked down. Faces were scrubbed. And mothers inspected everyone at the door before they could get in the car. Did you wash behind your ears? Where's your other glove? Don't get dirty before we get there.
scenes.caption: THE INSPECTION

scenes.text: Getting to church was part of the ritual. In small towns, families walked, greeting neighbors along the way. In the suburbs, they drove, and the church parking lot filled up with big shiny cars, many of them washed the day before just for this. Late arrivals tiptoed in during the first hymn, while everyone turned to look.
scenes.caption: GETTING TO CHURCH

scenes.text: In the nineteen fifties, church attendance in America was at a high point. Surveys at the time found that about half of all American adults attended religious services in a typical week. New churches were being built across the country, especially in the new suburbs. Sunday school classrooms overflowed with baby boom children.
scenes.caption: HALF OF ALL AMERICANS

scenes.text: Families sat in the same pew every week. Children were expected to sit still and be quiet, which was almost impossible. Mothers kept them in line with a look, a pinch, or a peppermint from her purse. Fathers sometimes dozed during the sermon. And everybody stood up and sat down at all the right times.
scenes.caption: THE SAME PEW

scenes.text: Children went to Sunday school, where they learned Bible stories from felt boards, colored pictures, memorized verses and sang songs. Jesus Loves Me. This Little Light of Mine. They got little cards with pictures for perfect attendance, and pins for every year without missing a Sunday.
scenes.caption: SUNDAY SCHOOL

scenes.text: And there was the collection plate. Children were given a coin, a nickel or a dime, to put in when the plate came down the pew. Some kept it in their shoe, or tied it in the corner of a handkerchief, so they wouldn't lose it. Many children learned their first lessons about giving from that little coin.
scenes.caption: THE COLLECTION PLATE

scenes.text: After the service, the congregation gathered outside on the church steps. Men shook hands with the minister and talked about the weather and the ballgame. Women admired each other's hats and new babies. Children ran around on the lawn in their good clothes, which was exactly what they had been told not to do.
scenes.caption: ON THE CHURCH STEPS

scenes.text: Faith was not the same for everyone, of course. Jewish families observed the Sabbath on Saturday. Catholic families went to Mass, often early in the morning, with the service still said in Latin. Many towns had a Methodist, a Baptist, a Lutheran and a Catholic church within a few blocks of each other. On Sunday morning, their bells rang at nearly the same time.
scenes.caption: THE BELLS RANG TOGETHER

scenes.text: Then home for Sunday dinner, the biggest meal of the week. In many families, it was served in the early afternoon, around one or two o'clock. The dining room table was set with the good tablecloth, the good china and the silver. It was the one meal of the week that was eaten in the dining room, not the kitchen.
scenes.caption: THE GOOD CHINA

scenes.text: The menu was usually the same. Pot roast with carrots and potatoes, or a roast chicken, or fried chicken, or a baked ham. Mashed potatoes and gravy. Green beans or peas. Homemade rolls with butter. A Jell-O salad. And a pie or a cake for dessert. Grandmothers often brought their specialty, and nobody else was allowed to make it.
scenes.caption: POT ROAST

scenes.text: Many families had grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins over every Sunday. Or they drove to Grandma's house. The children sat at a separate kids' table, often in the kitchen. The grown-ups talked about family news, politics and the price of everything. And somebody always said grace before anyone could eat.
scenes.caption: THE WHOLE FAMILY

scenes.text: After dinner, the women usually cleared the table and washed the dishes, talking in the kitchen. The men retired to the living room, loosened their ties, and settled into chairs. Within half an hour, many of them were asleep.
scenes.caption: THE DISHES

scenes.text: Children who finished their dinner asked to be excused, and ran outside, still in their good clothes. Older kids might be allowed to go to the afternoon matinee at the movie theater, if their parents approved of Sunday movies. Others were stuck in the living room with the grown-ups, listening to stories they had heard a hundred times.
scenes.caption: MAY I BE EXCUSED?

scenes.text: Outside, the town was quiet. In much of America in the nineteen fifties, stores were closed on Sunday. In many states and towns, so-called blue laws made it illegal to sell many things on Sunday. Car dealers, department stores and hardware stores were dark. In some places, even buying a hammer was against the law.
scenes.caption: THE BLUE LAWS

scenes.text: A few places stayed open. The drugstore, for medicine, might open for a few hours. Gas stations. Some restaurants. Movie theaters opened in the afternoon in many places. But in many states, liquor stores were closed, and so were bars. Main Street on a Sunday afternoon could look almost deserted.
scenes.caption: ALMOST DESERTED

scenes.text: Blue laws went back to colonial times, and many of them stayed on the books for decades. In nineteen sixty-one, the Supreme Court upheld them in a case called McGowan versus Maryland. It wasn't until the seventies and eighties that most states began to allow regular Sunday shopping.
scenes.caption: UPHELD IN 1961

scenes.text: Even radio and television felt different on Sunday. Mornings were full of religious programs, preachers and gospel choirs. Shows like The Lutheran Hour and Bishop Fulton Sheen's Life Is Worth Living drew millions of listeners and viewers. Sheen was so popular that he won an Emmy Award, and competed in the ratings with Milton Berle.
scenes.caption: LIFE IS WORTH LIVING

scenes.text: So what did families do on Sunday afternoon? Many went for a Sunday drive. The whole family piled into the car, with no particular destination. They drove into the countryside, past farms, lakes and fields, looking at the scenery. They might stop for an ice cream cone at a roadside stand, then drive home again.
scenes.caption: THE SUNDAY DRIVE

scenes.text: Others went visiting. Sunday afternoon was the time to call on relatives, neighbors and older friends. You dropped in without calling first, and you were always welcome. There would be coffee, a plate of cookies, and conversation on the porch or in the parlor.
scenes.caption: GOING VISITING

scenes.text: Children played outside, but often with special Sunday rules. In many religious homes, no rough games, no card playing, and no work on Sunday. Some families didn't even allow sewing or mowing the lawn on the Sabbath. Kids found ways to have fun anyway, with board games, reading, or quiet walks.
scenes.caption: SUNDAY RULES

scenes.text: In the fall, Sunday afternoon meant football on the radio, and increasingly, on television. Professional football was growing fast in the fifties. The famous nineteen fifty-eight championship game between the Baltimore Colts and the New York Giants, which went into overtime, was watched by millions and helped make the NFL a national passion.
scenes.caption: SUNDAY FOOTBALL

scenes.text: In summer, there might be a picnic in the park, a church social, or a baseball doubleheader at the local ballpark. Families packed fried chicken, potato salad and deviled eggs in a basket, spread a blanket under a tree, and spent the whole afternoon outdoors.
scenes.caption: THE PICNIC

scenes.text: And in the evening, many families went back to church for an evening service or youth group. Teenagers went to youth fellowship meetings, which were often as much about seeing friends as about religion. There were hymn sings, potluck suppers and, in summer, revival meetings in a tent at the edge of town.
scenes.caption: THE YOUTH GROUP

scenes.text: Sunday supper was light, since dinner had been so big. Leftovers, cold cuts, sandwiches, soup or popcorn. Sometimes just cereal or toast. Mothers needed a rest too, and Sunday evening was often the one meal of the week nobody really cooked.
scenes.caption: SUNDAY SUPPER

scenes.text: Then came Sunday night television, and it was the best night of the week. Lassie at seven. Then The Ed Sullivan Show at eight, which the whole family watched together. Ed Sullivan featured jugglers, comedians, opera singers, puppets and rock and roll stars, all in one hour. In September of nineteen fifty-six, about sixty million people watched Elvis Presley's first appearance on his show.
scenes.caption: THE ED SULLIVAN SHOW

scenes.text: After that, maybe Alfred Hitchcock Presents, or What's My Line? And then, the dreaded moment. Bedtime, and the realization that tomorrow was Monday. Homework that hadn't been done. School clothes laid out. Fathers polishing their shoes for work. Sunday was over.
scenes.caption: TOMORROW WAS MONDAY

scenes.text: So what happened to that kind of Sunday? Blue laws faded away. Stores opened. Malls opened. Families got busier. Both parents started working. Church attendance declined over the decades. Sports, shopping and errands filled up the day. And slowly, Sunday became just another day.
scenes.caption: JUST ANOTHER DAY

scenes.text: Many people today say they miss the old Sunday. Not necessarily the scratchy clothes or the strict rules, but the feeling of a day of rest. A day when the whole town slowed down. When nobody expected you to work. When the family sat at the same table, and had nowhere else to be.
scenes.caption: A DAY OF REST

scenes.text: If you grew up in the fifties, you remember Sunday. The church bells. The starched dress. The smell of pot roast. The drive in the country. Ed Sullivan. And that strange quiet over the whole town, as if the world had decided, just for one day, to take a deep breath.
scenes.caption: A DEEP BREATH

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. What did Sunday look like in your house growing up? What was always on the table for Sunday dinner, and what did your family do in the afternoon? We read every comment. And thank you, from all of us, for spending these last fifteen days with us. There's much more to come.
scenes.caption: WHAT WAS YOUR SUNDAY LIKE?
